selectedCourses.name: Personal & Professional Development
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
selectedCourses.contribution: Mandatory first-year academic literacy and personal/professional development.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

selectedCourses.name: Business & Economy in the Age of AI
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines AI's business, economic and societal implications without requiring a technical background. AI foundations and limitations lead into applications across enterprise functions and industries, labour-market change, productivity, innovation, market structure and inequality. Governance, corporate responsibility, regulation and future scenarios connect technological developments to institutional choices. Students analyze business cases and competing scholarly arguments, then investigate a country's AI readiness, workforce, regulation and industrial policy.
selectedCourses.contribution: examines AI effects on labour markets, inequality, HR, governance and organisational change, directly contributing to technology and work questions
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Examines AI's business, economic and societal implications without requiring a technical background. Students study AI's capabilities and limits, applications across business functions and industries, and effects on labour markets, productivity, innovation and inequality. Business cases and scholarly arguments support analysis of governance, regulation and a country's AI readiness and industrial policy.

selectedCourses.name: Introduction to Economics
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces microeconomic principles and short-run macroeconomic analysis. The microeconomic component examines supply and demand, strategic interaction, consumer choice, production, costs and competitive markets. The macroeconomic component introduces output, unemployment and inflation, then relates goods and financial markets through the IS-LM model. Students use algebra and graphs to explain economic behaviour and apply models to economic issues.
selectedCourses.contribution: examines markets, firms, unemployment and inflation as economic mechanisms shaping work and institutions; it does not claim to teach demography or family sociology
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.

selectedCourses.name: Microeconomics & Behavior
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Develops microeconomic theory through consumer behaviour, imperfectly competitive markets and economy-wide allocation. Students examine choice under uncertainty, non-egoistic preferences and cognitive limitations, then monopoly, strategic behaviour and labour and capital markets. General equilibrium, efficiency, externalities and government complete the analysis. Algebraic problem-solving and graphical analysis are connected to the interpretation and evaluation of research papers.
selectedCourses.contribution: examines individual and producer decisions, market structures, factor markets and regulation, supplying economic mechanisms to compare with structural sociological explanations
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Study how consumers and producers make decisions under scarcity. Explore key concepts such as rational choice, decision-making under uncertainty, and non-egoistic preferences. Analyze market structures, strategic interactions, and factor markets. Learn how markets function and examine the impact of regulation. Develop analytical tools to better understand behavior and engage with empirical research.

selectedCourses.name: Public Economics
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines government intervention through the efficiency and equity effects of public policy. Market failure, public goods and externalities provide foundations for studying public production, collective choice, spending and taxation. Health, education, welfare and social insurance illustrate expenditure and redistribution questions. Students apply economic models, interpret data and graphs, evaluate research and develop a research proposal and paper.
selectedCourses.contribution: examines taxation, redistribution and public intervention relevant to inequality and policy
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.

selectedCourses.name: Research Methods & Statistics
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.
selectedCourses.contribution: provides quantitative research design and statistical methods
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Research Methods & Statistics introduces research design, operationalisation, measurement, sampling, surveys and experiments. Students study descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression using R and R Commander. A group project develops a research plan and instruments, collects and analyses data, and reports findings under research-ethics and privacy requirements.

selectedCourses.name: Psychology of Leading Under Pressure
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines how emotion regulation, emotional intelligence, emotional expression and suppression, emotional labor, belonging, identity safety and psychological safety shape leadership and social interaction under conflict, exclusion and interpersonal uncertainty. It emphasises inclusive leadership and ethnic, cultural, sexual and gender minority experiences, with digital emotion regulation as a further strand. Students conduct a supervised quantitative survey project: formulating theory-driven hypotheses, selecting established psychological measures, designing and piloting a Qualtrics survey, recruiting participants ethically, collecting original data and preparing a clean dataset. Individual work applies descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlations, group comparisons and introductory multiple regression in SPSS or RStudio, and interprets findings and limitations in empirical reports and evidence-based leadership recommendations.
selectedCourses.contribution: Examines inclusive leadership, identity safety, belonging and minority experiences under pressure. A supervised quantitative survey and empirical report investigate these mechanisms of organisational inclusion; this is not a broad diversity-management syllabus.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Examines how emotion regulation, emotional intelligence, belonging, identity safety and psychological safety shape leadership in diverse contexts, with particular attention to minority experiences. Students design and pilot a quantitative survey, collect data ethically, and use SPSS or RStudio for descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlations, group comparisons and introductory multiple regression. They interpret the findings and develop evidence-based leadership recommendations.

selectedCourses.name: Psychology of Organizations & Leadership
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines organizational behaviour at individual, group and organizational levels. Topics connect personality, perception, emotions and motivation to teams, leadership, power, conflict, structure, culture and change. Students design research plans for organizational cases and conduct a brief systematic literature review using PRISMA reporting tools. Workshops develop literature searching, study selection, source appraisal and synthesis, linking organizational-psychology evidence to practical questions and recommendations.
selectedCourses.contribution: studies workplace attitudes, motivation, power, groups, organisational culture and structure as a specific account of work and institutional change
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Psychology of Organizations & Leadership examines the psychological, social and structural dynamics of organisations. Case discussions and research-based frameworks address motivation, leadership, group dynamics, organisational culture, power, conflict and change.

selectedCourses.name: AI Ethics
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines AI through ethical theory and psychological accounts of human behaviour and interaction. Ethical debates address fairness, privacy, responsibility, alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Psychological perspectives consider development, clinical care, social and organizational relationships, forensic applications and cognitive neuroscience. Students synthesize literature and apply ethical frameworks in an analytical psychology project and a research-grounded podcast, with a creative communication component.
selectedCourses.contribution: examines AI fairness, bias, responsibility, agency and algorithmic effects in organisational and social life as substantive questions about technology and society
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: AI Ethics examines artificial intelligence from philosophical and psychological perspectives. Topics include fairness, privacy, responsibility, human-value alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Students apply ethical frameworks to questions about human behaviour and interaction, synthesise research in an analytical psychology project, and produce a research-based podcast.

selectedCourses.name: Introduction to Data Science
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.
selectedCourses.contribution: teaches data cleaning, manipulation, visualisation and project-based analysis with datasets from social sciences and other fields; it is a general empirical tool rather than a prescribed sociology project
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.

selectedCourses.name: Governance of Sustainability
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Analyzes sustainability as a problem of collective decision-making involving governments, markets and civil society. Concepts of institutions, power, participation, justice and problem complexity frame competing technological and systemic responses. Structured cases examine food, freshwater, energy and climate mitigation. Students apply governance frameworks to a Zeeland issue, consult relevant organizations or experts, and produce policy advice or an evaluation assessing effectiveness, feasibility and stakeholder interests.
selectedCourses.contribution: examines governance arrangements for sustainability transitions
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.

selectedCourses.name: Sustainability Essentials I
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Uses planetary boundaries to introduce scientific tools for understanding sustainability and human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and learn chemical, thermodynamic and mechanical principles relevant to environmental processes. Topics connect climate, ocean acidification, nutrient cycles, energy and materials. An iterative laboratory project makes starch-based biopolymers and measures their strength and elasticity to improve the formulation.
selectedCourses.contribution: introduces planetary boundaries and the environmental limits within which human development occurs, grounding the selected environmental-assessment work
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Introduces sustainability through planetary boundaries and scientific tools for understanding human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and study chemical and physical principles relevant to climate, energy and materials. A laboratory project makes and tests starch-based biopolymers.

selectedCourses.name: Climate Change
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces climate-change science, societal impacts, and mitigation and adaptation. Students examine greenhouse gases, feedbacks, tipping points, ocean acidification and sea-level rise, then consequences for ecosystems, agriculture, transport, buildings and health. Climate justice, governance, communication and misinformation connect physical changes to social responses. Solution pathways include energy systems, carbon removal and climate-adaptive planning. Students interview a stakeholder and produce a short film, alongside reflection on their own role.
selectedCourses.contribution: provides scientific grounding in climate change for analysing climate-society relations
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.

selectedCourses.name: Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Develops life-cycle approaches to evaluating products, processes and services within a circular economy. Students examine environmental, social and health consequences from resource extraction to disposal or reuse, together with costs, revenues and management strategies. Three preliminary projects develop different parts or forms of life-cycle analysis, followed by a project that integrates the stages into a full product or process assessment.
selectedCourses.contribution: evaluates environmental, social and health consequences of products and services across their life cycle, supplying an explicit assessment method for societal transitions
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Teaches evaluation of environmental impacts of products, processes and services throughout their lifecycle. Emphasises strategic planning for a circular economy through hands‑on learning.

selectedCourses.name: Law, Society & Justice
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces law through legal, social and normative perspectives. Students compare major legal traditions and survey public and private law, including constitutional, criminal, international, human-rights, property, contract and tort law. The second part examines justice, social control and change, race and gender. Case briefs, legal interpretation, demand letters and mock trials apply legal reasoning; a family-law topic supports the design of a small socio-legal research proposal.
selectedCourses.contribution: provides a foundation in how law structures society and justice
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Law, Society & Justice examines legal, social and normative perspectives on law. Students compare legal traditions and study public and private law, human rights, justice, social control and change, race and gender. Case briefs, demand letters and mock trials develop legal reasoning, while a family-law topic supports the design of a socio-legal research proposal.

selectedCourses.name: Modern History
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Surveys economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present while questioning the meaning and periodization of modernity. Students examine industrialization, political ideologies, nationalism, imperialism, migration, world wars, revolution, decolonization, the Cold War and globalization. Historical research and essays connect specific questions to evidence. A group project analyzes historical visions of the future as products of their own contexts and compares them with subsequent developments.
selectedCourses.contribution: examines industrialisation, political revolutions, welfare states and decolonisation as specific historical transformations of social institutions
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.

selectedCourses.name: Histories of Gender
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Studies gendered histories and lives in North America from the nineteenth century to the present, centering storytelling and intersectionality. Queer and heteronormative narratives connect slavery, family, sexuality, health, incarceration and contemporary backlash to resistance and activism. Students interpret primary sources and scholarship, interview older queer people, contribute to the Walking with Pride activist artwork, and conduct an original research project in a chosen format.
selectedCourses.contribution: examines gendered institutions, marginalisation, activism and cultural representations through historical research and interviews; this is a historical case of identity and inequality, not a general culture survey
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Studies gender, storytelling and marginalised lives in the nineteenth- to twenty-first-century American context. Students examine slavery, community activism, representation and lived experience, using sources and projects that connect historical interpretation with contemporary questions.

selectedCourses.name: Native American Histories
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Studies Native American social and cultural histories from the nineteenth century to the present through Indigenous perspectives and collaborative inquiry. Boarding schools, institutional violence, family separation and intergenerational trauma are connected to contemporary resistance, resurgence, food sovereignty and cultural expression. Storytelling, relational accountability and reciprocity inform work with Indigenous peers and knowledge holders. Arts-based collaborations and a public-history project develop respectful, accessible accounts of historical and contemporary issues.
selectedCourses.contribution: examines Indigenous histories, forced schooling, cultural resistance, migration, trauma and family life using social/cultural history and Indigenous methodologies; this is a substantive historical case of exclusion and institutional power

selectedCourses.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Studies human rights both as positive law and as philosophical claims. Students examine the UDHR, European and UN protection systems, monitoring institutions and landmark cases alongside natural law, natural rights, legal positivism and critiques of universality. Historical and philosophical texts frame debates about dignity, life and reproductive rights, punishment, religious freedom, expression and democracy. Close engagement with legal and philosophical arguments supports independent moral positions.
selectedCourses.contribution: connects rights and normative justice to social inequality
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.

selectedCourses.name: Comparative Constitutional Law
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Compares constitutional structures, institutions and rights across legal systems and introduces administrative law. Students examine constitutional features, federalism, legislatures, executive relationships, courts, judicial review and human rights. The administrative component addresses public participation, remedies and procedural fairness. A staged booklet compares two constitutions, supported by legal interpretation, case-law analysis and application of principles to hypothetical facts.

selectedCourses.name: Ethics
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Studies moral reasoning through historical and contemporary ethical theories and close philosophical reading. Utilitarianism, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics lead into Nietzsche's genealogy, Murdoch's account of goodness and Nagel's treatments of value, perspective, death and meaning. Reflection and research essays require interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.

selectedCourses.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics

Students study political institutions, rules, actors and behaviour, including parties, elections, participation, polarization, interest groups and policy. A qualitative or quantitative research memo answers a theoretically grounded comparative-politics question through empirical analysis.
selectedCourses.contribution: provides comparative institutional analysis of political systems
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Provides analytical tools to compare political systems and democracies. Examines phenomena like democratic backsliding, decline of political parties, rise of populism, media changes, non‑majoritarian institutions and globalization’s impact on domestic politics.

selectedCourses.name: Theory of International Relations

selectedCourses.name: Introduction to Sociology
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline. Students connect solidarity, modernity, identity, social boundaries, networks and stratification to race, gender, migration and inequality in education and work. An individual analysis applies a course concept to contemporary social life without original data collection. A group paper develops a sociological question and analyzes a social problem using theory and academic literature.

selectedCourses.name: Qualitative Research Methodology

Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
selectedCourses.contribution: provides dedicated qualitative research design and interviewing methodology
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.

selectedCourses.name: Modern Sociology
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines twentieth-century and contemporary social theory alongside critical accounts of modernity, colonialism and disciplinary exclusion. Functionalism, critical theory, Black feminist thought, phenomenology, symbolic interactionism and Bourdieu's work are read with postcolonial, decolonial and Indigenous perspectives. Students compare theories and apply them to empirical cases, including visual material. An individual research paper develops a theoretically grounded interpretation of a selected social phenomenon.
selectedCourses.contribution: examines modern sociological theory and colonial histories, developing the disciplinary foundation for contemporary social theory
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.

selectedCourses.name: Social Movements & Environmental Justice
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.

selectedCourses.contribution: examines framing, persuasion and public discourse and applies communication research with local organisations; it complements rather than replaces the full sociology practice component
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Persuasive Communication studies persuasion through communication studies, social psychology and ethical analysis. Students examine framing, argumentation, cognitive shortcuts and verbal and nonverbal communication. Community-engaged projects develop communication encouraging sustainable and circular lifestyles, while an individual research paper evaluates selected persuasion tools.

reusedSharedDescriptionReview.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Revised the description to retain supported academic scope and activities without superseded or unsupported details.

removedCourseEvidence.evidenceRead: This course integrates insights from psychology into economic theory to better understand how people make decisions. Learn how actual behavior deviates from the predictions of traditional economic models due to biases, heuristics, and framing. Through experiments, students will deepen their understanding of decision-making and its implications for economic theory and practice.

Introduces the EU legal order through its institutions, sources, competences and relationship to member-state law. Students study supremacy, legal effect, liability and judicial remedies before applying citizenship and free-movement law to concrete problems. Structured legal cases and research into current judgments develop interpretation and comparison across EU and domestic settings. Digital regulation and the green transition provide a contemporary application.

Provides a research-project setting for sustainability questions supplied by organizations and companies in the Zeeland delta. Small teams work with an external advisor to review literature, formulate a research question, plan and execute an investigation, and develop a final product, design or report. The substantive topic and practical techniques depend on the partner project; the common focus is an evidence-based research process and engagement with external stakeholders.

Introduces computational problem-solving and programming in Python. Students develop structured programs using branching, iteration, functions and data collections, then progress to recursion, exception handling and object-oriented programming with inheritance. Elements of logic, sets and enumeration support computational reasoning. Exercises and projects require students to write, trace, test, debug and explain programs that solve problems of moderate complexity.

conceptJudgments: Sociological theory (intro/modern/civil society), qualitative research, statistics and empirical social/policy inquiries directly respond to defining sociology substance. Economics, public health, political/historical inquiry have specific explanatory roles; not generic breadth.

Rights, institutional power, minority inclusion, Indigenous/gender histories and sociology implement inequality/social change with legal and historical methods. Five-course difference is a material rights/institutional shift, not threshold filler.

Social theory and methods anchor technology/work and environmental transitions. Climate/LCA supply factual impact methods; governance, public economics and policy analysis study collective responses. AI ethics/business/organisational study have actual institutional/work content. No assumed sociological partner project or incidental technical topic defines the concept.
implementationFinding: Four original unavailable placements required repair. Public Policy Analysis replaces behavioral economics, EU law and project-based sustainability research in the respective alternatives for direct policy substance. Research Delta is only planned at the outset, before research foundations; its unknown partner topic cannot guarantee sociology-specific research. A trial retaining Python programming produced an infeasible term allocation. Public Economics is a stronger concept-supported instrument/redistribution contribution and makes the third schedule feasible. No availability restored; no no-match inferred from planning. Advisory foundations soft, zero slack for preferred sociology order.

alignments.rationale: Both courses introduce sociology's central concepts, classical theories and methods for analysing social relations and institutions; the UCR course is a direct disciplinary counterpart.

Modern Sociology engages major sociological theories and debates about modernity, providing a direct counterpart to the comparator's study of foundational sociological texts, though it organises the material as a modern-theory course rather than a key-texts survey.
Qualitative Research Methodology directly covers research design, qualitative data collection, interpretation, dissemination and researcher positionality in the study of social processes.

Statistics & Experimental Methods directly develops multivariate statistical analysis, model selection, execution and reporting for research in sociology and adjacent fields. Its experimental and behavioural-science framing is narrower than a full sociology-specific quantitative-methods sequence.

New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory directly studies advanced global debates in sociological theory, including civil society, solidarity, social trust and decolonial critique. Its thematic focus is narrower than the comparator's general theoretical-sociology component.

Social Movements & Environmental Justice examines structural inequality, exclusion and collective responses through environmental-justice cases. It therefore covers a substantial applied part of the broader social-inequality component rather than its full sociological scope.

Foundations of Comparative Politics directly introduces political institutions, regimes and comparative empirical analysis. It covers a central political-science domain while placing more emphasis on comparative politics than a general political-science survey.

Histories of Gender examines identities, marginalisation, gendered institutions and cultural representation through historical inquiry and interviews. It is a substantial historical case-based counterpart to culture and identity, with narrower thematic and geographical scope; generic social psychology was the weaker previous placement.

Peace & Conflict directly examines the causes and dynamics of conflict, structural inequality, identity-based grievances and peacebuilding. It covers the conflict side of the broader cohesion-and-conflict component, while giving less attention to social cohesion outside conflict settings.

Research Methods & Statistics directly teaches research design, operationalisation, sampling and empirical project planning. It also adds introductory statistics, so it is broader methodologically than the comparator's research-design component.

Public Policy Analysis directly studies policy-making processes and competing policy conceptualisations across national and international settings, with policy memos. Its single sugar-policy case is narrower than the broader introductory policy component.

Climate change, societal impacts, justice, governance and mitigation/adaptation directly address the environmental-change side of planetary sociology. Substantial physical science and a climate focus differ from its broader sociological framing.
No scheduled course reproduces a specifically sociological 15-EC research project. Generic project work does not establish that disciplinary research relationship.

Personal & Professional Development explicitly develops critical source analysis, academic writing, presentations, collaboration and reflection. It is a stronger broad academic-skills counterpart than the specialised persuasion course; the external 8-EC Skills component also contains discipline-specific research and policy skills.

Psychology of Organizations & Leadership examines organisational structure, culture, groups, power and management. This provides a stronger substantial organisational counterpart than the former entrepreneurship/startup course; its psychological emphasis differs from the broad external organisation-and-management course.

Introduction to Economics provides useful background on markets, firms and unemployment but does not directly study population change, family relations and work as a sociological and demographic field. No scheduled UCR course is a sufficiently direct counterpart.

The comparator component focuses specifically on urban sociology and migration. The scheduled UCR courses provide related political, historical and sociological context but no course directly combines cities and migration as its principal subject.
The comparator requires a 15-EC placement in professional sociological practice. No scheduled UCR course constitutes an internship or reproduces that sustained placement function.

The comparator reserves 15 EC as a formal minor or exchange block. UCR's open curriculum offers choice throughout the programme but no scheduled course represents an equivalent reserved profiling block.

Onderzoek in de Praktijk translates sociological research into professional practice and communication for a chosen field. Several UCR courses contain applied or community-engaged work, but none has this specific sociology-to-practice function.

The Bachelor Project is a 15-EC independently executed sociological study. None of the 24 scheduled UCR courses is an equivalent bachelor thesis or independent capstone, so the component remains unmatched.

alignmentFinding: All 21 component placements and 36 UCR rows reviewed. Policy analysis is stronger than economic policy alone. The generic research-project function is removed as a positive match. Climate–planetary relationship retains specific societal/climate-justice/governance overlap with physical-science limitation. Gender histories directly study identity but are narrower. Dedicated urban/demographic sociology, internship, sociological research project/practice and thesis remain gaps. Optional research additional and unscheduled.
